subject: science
passage: In some cities, carrion crows have been seen placing walnuts on roads so that passing cars will crack the hard shells. Biologist Mi-rae Choi observed that the crows she studied placed nuts at pedestrian crosswalks far more often than elsewhere along the same roads. She hypothesizes that the crows favor crosswalks because traffic there halts at regular intervals when the signals change, allowing the birds to walk out and collect the cracked nuts without the risk of being struck by a car.
stem: Which finding, if true, would most directly weaken Choi's hypothesis?

choices.A: Crows that placed nuts at crosswalks collected them sooner than crows that placed nuts elsewhere.
choices.B: In the countryside, crows of the same species crack nuts by dropping them onto rocks.
choices.C: Crows placed nuts just as often at crosswalks whose broken signals never stopped traffic.
choices.D: Cars passing over the crosswalks cracked most of the nuts that the crows placed there.

explanation.why: Choi's hypothesis names a specific reason for the crosswalk preference: the regular pauses in traffic. If crows favor crosswalks just as much when the signals are broken and traffic never pauses, the pauses cannot be what draws them.
explanation.A: Incorrect. Quicker collection at crosswalks fits the idea that pauses in traffic make retrieval easier, so this supports Choi.
explanation.B: Incorrect. How crows crack nuts in the countryside says nothing about why city crows prefer crosswalks.
explanation.C: Correct. The preference survives when the pauses are removed, so the pauses are unlikely to explain it.
explanation.D: Incorrect. This shows that cars crack the nuts, which the text already states; it does not address why crosswalks are chosen.
